findings.who: A filer who is legally married at the end of 2025 but files as head of household because they are 'considered unmarried' (they lived apart from their spouse for the last six months of the year). The estranged spouse was on active duty in the U.S. armed forces in 2025, and the filer never served.
findings.why_no: The federal head-of-household rules tell this filer they are 'considered unmarried', so they answer no to 'Married at the end of 2025 and not filing a joint return'. They also truthfully answer no to the federal armed-forces question, which asks only about 'you' when the return is not joint. The gate is then false, so the spouse's active duty is never asked about.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: 'Note: Special rules under the SCRA apply to members of the military and their spouses for determining residency.'
findings.fix: Base the married helper on legal marital status, not filing status. For example: 'Were you legally married on December 31, 2025, even if you file as head of household or are considered unmarried for federal purposes, and not filing a joint return?' Or ask the active-duty question directly of anyone who was married at any time in 2025.

findings.who: A filer whose spouse died during 2025 after serving on active duty that year. The filer files separately rather than jointly, for example because an executor files the decedent's return.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'Married at the end of 2025' literally and answers no because the spouse had died before year end. Federal rules, however, treat them as married for all of 2025. The armed-forces question on their non-joint return asks only about themselves, so they answer no there too.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: 'Note: Special rules under the SCRA apply to members of the military and their spouses for determining residency.'
findings.fix: Word the helper as 'Were you married at any time in 2025 (including a spouse who died during 2025) and not filing a joint return?', or widen the gate to anyone married at any time in 2025.

findings.who: A filer who was in active federal service in 2025 in a role they do not count as 'armed forces, Coast Guard, reserves or National Guard', such as a recalled retiree or a member of the Individual Ready Reserve called to active duty.
findings.why_no: The filer reads the federal list as covering only current units and does not see their own recall as 'serving'.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: 'whether or not you were domiciled in New York State (unless you were in active service in the military)'
findings.fix: Add help to the federal question: 'Include any active duty in 2025, including a retiree recalled to service or a member of the Individual Ready Reserve.'

findings.who: A Yonkers resident, or a self-employed filer in the MCTA region who pays the metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax (MCTMT) by estimated payments. They want part of the overpayment to cover 2026 Yonkers surcharge or MCTMT estimates.
findings.why_no: "Your 2026 New York tax" may read as New York State income tax only. The filer may enter zero, or a smaller amount, thinking the Yonkers or MCTMT estimate cannot be paid from the refund.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Ask: "How much of your New York overpayment should be applied to your 2026 estimated tax (New York State, New York City, Yonkers and MCTMT)?"

findings.who: A filer who directs part of the overpayment to NYS 529 accounts on Form IT-195 (line 78a).
findings.why_no: The help says "The rest is refunded to you." The filer may lower or misjudge the line 79 amount, thinking the remainder all comes back as a refund. The instructions say lines 78a through 79 together should equal line 77.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "The total of lines 78a through 79 should equal the amount on line 77."
findings.fix: Help: "The rest goes to any NYS 529 deposits you choose and is otherwise refunded to you."

findings.who: Spouses filing jointly who plan to make 2026 estimated payments, or where only the spouse expects 2026 self-employment or MCTMT liability.
findings.why_no: "Your 2026 New York tax" may read as the asking spouse's own tax only, so the couple may apply less than they intend.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: On joint returns, say "your and your spouse's 2026 estimated tax".

findings.who: A New York City resident buys furniture in a lower-rate New York county, such as one at 8%, pays that county's tax, and brings it home to NYC (8.875%). The same applies when a seller ships to a NY address but charges the rate of the wrong locality.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether they bought anything 'without paying New York sales tax, such as online or out of state'. They paid New York sales tax, and the purchase was neither online nor out of state, so no is truthful. Only the help mentions a purchase 'taxed below the combined state and local rate', and the examples steer away from purchases inside New York.
findings.line: ny_it201.use_tax_dmv_only_if_bought (forced false), so no use tax goes to IT-201 line 59 although the difference in locality rates is owed
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You owe use tax to the second locality if you were a resident of that locality at the time of the purchase, and its rate of tax is higher than the rate of tax originally paid.'
findings.fix: Widen the question: 'In 2025, did you (or your spouse) buy anything taxable that you used in New York without paying the full sales tax rate of the place in New York where you lived, including a purchase where tax was charged at a lower rate (another state, another NY county, or a seller that charged too little)?'

findings.who: A Manhattan resident buys a laptop in Pennsylvania, pays 6% Pennsylvania sales tax, and brings it home.
findings.why_no: They did pay sales tax, and read 'without paying New York sales tax' as 'without paying sales tax'. The rule that tax paid elsewhere only earns a credit, and the rest is still owed, appears only in help they may skip.
findings.line: ny_it201.use_tax_dmv_only_if_bought (forced false); line 59 omits the use tax that remains after the credit
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'purchased an item or service outside New York State that is subject to tax in New York State ... with subsequent use in New York State' and 'You may be entitled to a credit for sales tax paid to another state.'
findings.fix: Put it in the question: 'Count a purchase even if another state charged tax, when its rate was lower than your New York rate.'

findings.who: A filer buys digital software, prewritten software downloads, or taxable services such as information services or out-of-state repair of property kept in NY. Sellers charged no tax.
findings.why_no: The question asks the filer to decide what is 'taxable in New York'. Many people assume downloads and services are not taxable, or that they only buy 'things', so they answer no.
findings.line: ny_it201.use_tax_dmv_only_if_bought (forced false); line 59 drops the chart amount or the ST-141 amount
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You owe sales or compensating use tax if you: purchased an item or service subject to tax that is delivered to you in New York State without payment of New York State and local tax to the seller'
findings.fix: Ask about a fact the filer can check: 'Did any online, catalog, TV, out-of-state or reservation seller (including software and services) not charge you New York tax?' Classify taxability after a yes.

findings.who: A landlord with rental real estate, or a holder of royalty interests, not registered for sales tax, buys appliances or equipment for the rental from an out-of-state seller who charges no tax.
findings.why_no: The filer sees these as business or rental costs, not personal purchases. The help's 'Leave out purchases of a business' reads as covering them, although only a business registered for sales tax is excluded.
findings.line: ny_it201.use_tax_dmv_only_if_bought (forced false); line 59 omits use tax that must be computed on ST-141
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You must use Form ST-141 ... if ... You owe sales or use tax for purchases related to a business not registered for sales tax purposes, rental real estate, or royalty activities.'
findings.fix: State it: 'Include purchases for a rental property, royalty activity, or a business that is not registered to collect sales tax.'

findings.who: A resident buys an item out of state in late December 2024 and first brings it into New York or uses it there in 2025. Or an order placed in 2024 is delivered in 2025.
findings.why_no: 'In 2025, did you ... buy' points to the purchase date, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'purchased an item or service outside New York State ... with subsequent use in New York State'
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2025, did you buy, receive, or first bring into New York anything ...' and add 'unless you already reported it on an earlier return'.

findings.who: A commuter domiciled in Connecticut, New Jersey or Westchester who keeps a Manhattan apartment all year and spends 184 or more days (counting part days) in New York City.
findings.why_no: "Did you live in New York City ... for all of 2025?" asks where the filer lived. The help covers only time away from a city home. This filer's home is in the suburbs, so the truthful answer is no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more in New York State"; p. 31: "substitute New York City or Yonkers in place of New York State"
findings.fix: Ask about the statutory test directly. First ask whether the filer (or spouse) kept a place to live in New York City for nearly all of 2025. If yes, ask how many days, counting any part of a day, they spent in the city. Treat a city resident as anyone domiciled in the city or meeting both parts of the test, then route on that result.

findings.who: A filer domiciled in New York City who spent all of 2025 on a temporary work assignment in Atlanta or abroad. They sublet or gave up the city apartment, plan to return, and visited the city more than 30 days, so the Group A exception does not apply.
findings.why_no: The help counts time away only "if your home stayed in the city". With no city apartment, the filer did not "live" in the city at all in 2025 and answers no. Their domicile is still the city.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "If you move to a new location but intend to stay there only for a limited amount of time (no matter how long), your domicile does not change." Also: "Your domicile is New York State. However ... you are not a resident if you meet all three of the conditions in either Group A or Group B"
findings.fix: Ask separately whether the filer's permanent home, the place they intend to return to, was in New York City all year, even if they lived elsewhere temporarily. Apply the Group A and Group B exceptions only after a yes.

findings.who: A filer who moved from Brooklyn to Florida in 2025 but kept the Brooklyn apartment, kept their job ties and family in the city, and expects to come back. The move does not meet the clear-and-convincing standard for a change of domicile.
findings.why_no: The filer reads "for all of 2025" by the calendar: they moved out in the spring, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "A change of domicile is clear and convincing only when your primary ties are clearly greater in the new location." Also: "Your New York domicile does not change until you can demonstrate that you have abandoned your New York domicile"
findings.fix: After a no, ask whether the filer moved away from the city in 2025. If so, ask whether they kept their city home and their main ties there. If they did, treat them as still domiciled in the city, or refer them for a domicile review.

findings.who: A graduate, law or medical student, or a full-time undergraduate's spouse, who is domiciled elsewhere and lives all year in university housing in Manhattan, spending more than 184 days in the city.
findings.why_no: The help says "A college dorm does not count as a home." The student reads it as covering every student residence and answers no. The exclusion applies only to full-time undergraduates in a baccalaureate program.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "a residence maintained by a full-time student enrolled at an institution of higher education in an undergraduate degree program leading to a baccalaureate degree and occupied by the student while attending the institution is not a permanent place of abode with respect to that student"
findings.fix: Change the help to: "Housing you occupied as a full-time undergraduate student working toward a bachelor's degree does not count as a place to live. Graduate students' university housing does count."

findings.who: A commuter who keeps a city apartment and counts only nights slept there (for example 150). Counting every workday they set foot in the city, they reach more than 184 days.
findings.why_no: Neither the gate help nor the State question help says that any part of a day counts as a day. The filer counts nights and decides they did not live in the city.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "*Any part of a day is a day for this purpose."
findings.fix: Ask for a day count with this help: "Count every day you were in New York City for any part of the day, including commuting days."

findings.who: A joint filer who moved into the city mid-2025 while their spouse lived in the city all year, or who lived in the city all year while the spouse lived elsewhere.
findings.why_no: The gate says "you", while the line's helper tests "you (and your spouse, on a joint return)". Spouses with different residency statuses may need different handling for the joint return, and the gate question does not ask about the spouse.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "A permanent place of abode usually includes a residence your spouse owns or leases." Also, Group B: "You, your spouse (unless legally separated) and minor children spent 90 days or less"
findings.fix: Ask the gate as "Did you and your spouse each ...", record each spouse's answer, and route mixed answers to the part-year or nonresident path.

findings.who: A member of the military, or a military spouse, whose legal residence is New York City but who is stationed or living elsewhere.
findings.why_no: The filer has not lived in the city for the year and answers no. Their residency is governed by special SCRA rules that the gate does not mention.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "Note: Special rules under the SCRA apply to members of the military and their spouses for determining residency."
findings.fix: Add a screening question: "Were you or your spouse in active military service, or a military spouse, in 2025?" Route a yes to the military residency rules.

findings.who: A Yonkers resident who made only 2025 Yonkers estimated income tax payments, with no New York State, New York City, or MCTMT estimated payments.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'New York income tax,' and the help lists only 'State, City or commuter (MCTMT)' tax; it never names Yonkers, so the filer reads the list as complete and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22, Line 75: 'your 2025 estimated tax payments for New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax'
findings.fix: Add 'Yonkers' to the gate and help, or ask broadly whether the filer made any 2025 New York State, New York City, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax payment.

findings.who: A beneficiary of an estate or trust that paid 2025 New York estimated tax and allocated the beneficiary's share on the required notification, but did not distribute cash to the beneficiary.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'have estimated tax passed to you'; the filer reads 'passed' as money distributed to them, not as an allocation of estimated tax paid on their behalf, and the help does not mention estate or trust allocations.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 22, Line 75: 'your portion of any payment of estimated taxes allocated to you by the estate or trust' and 'submit a copy of the notification issued by the estate or trust'
findings.fix: Say 'or had an estate or trust allocate or pay estimated tax on your behalf, even if you received no cash,' and mention the notification in the help.

findings.who: A married couple filing a joint IT-201. Only the spouse bought an untaxed item, for example a laptop delivered to their Monroe County home by an out-of-state seller who collected no New York tax.
findings.why_no: The gate is worded for one person ('rate where you lived in New York'). The filer did not buy anything untaxed and truthfully answers no.
findings.line: ny_it201.gate.use_tax_abode (and line 59 itself, which the same gate zeroes)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: 'You owe sales or compensating use tax if you: • purchased an item or service subject to tax that is delivered to you in New York State without payment of New York State and local tax to the seller'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse buy goods or services ...' for every per-return use-tax question.

findings.who: A New York resident who bought untaxed cigarettes, fuel or other goods on an Indian reservation in New York (not an Oneida Nation purchase), or bought from a television shopping channel that charged no New York tax.
findings.why_no: The examples are 'online, by catalog, or out of state and brought into New York'. A reservation purchase made inside New York, or a TV-channel order, does not match them, and the filer takes the list as complete.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'An unpaid sales or use tax liability commonly occurs if you made purchases through the Internet, by catalog, from television shopping channels, or on an Indian reservation (except for purchases subject to Oneida Nation taxes)'
findings.fix: Add to the examples 'from a television shopping channel, or on an Indian reservation in New York (other than Oneida Nation purchases)', and say the list is not complete.

findings.who: A New York resident who bought goods abroad and brought them home or had them shipped through customs, paying foreign VAT but no New York tax.
findings.why_no: 'Out of state' reads as another U.S. state. Having paid tax abroad, the filer believes they did pay sales tax.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'purchased an item or service outside New York State that is subject to tax in New York State (and you were a resident of New York State at the time of purchase) with subsequent use in New York State' ... 'routine audits based on information received from third parties, including the U.S. Customs Service'
findings.fix: Say 'outside New York State, including in another country', and state that foreign VAT or other foreign tax is not New York sales tax.

findings.who: A resident who ordered items online from sellers that collected no tax, or paid an out-of-state shop to repair an item, and cannot tell whether those purchases are 'taxable in New York'.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for a legal classification ('goods or services taxable in New York'). Unsure filers assume online purchases or services are not taxable and answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Example 1: 'You purchased a computer over the Internet that was delivered to your house in Monroe County, New York, from an out-of-state company and did not pay sales tax to that company.'
findings.fix: First ask a fact the filer can check: 'Did you or your spouse buy anything delivered to or brought into New York on which the seller charged no New York sales tax, or a lower rate than your New York locality?' Settle taxability afterwards, with guidance.

findings.who: A resident who paid sales tax in another state, or in a lower-rate New York locality, on an item brought home to a higher-rate New York locality where they lived at the time of purchase.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks 'I paid sales tax' and does not compare rates. The lower-rate clause sits in a long sentence and is easy to miss.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18: 'You owe use tax to the second locality if you were a resident of that locality at the time of the purchase, and its rate of tax is higher than the rate of tax originally paid.'
findings.fix: Ask the lower-rate case as its own question: 'Did you pay sales tax somewhere else at a lower rate than where you lived in New York?'

findings.who: A New York City resident who filed a joint federal return but does not know where the spouse is. The spouse left during or before 2025 and cannot be found despite reasonable efforts.
findings.why_no: The filer cannot truthfully say the spouse 'also live[d] in New York City for all of 2025', because they do not know where the spouse lived. The residence gate excludes exactly the case the gated question exists for.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 5, Item A: "You are unable to file a joint New York return because: – the address or whereabouts of your spouse is unknown ... In this case, you may file a separate New York return"
findings.fix: Ask the cannot-sign question of every filer who was married and filed a joint federal return, before and independent of the spouse-residence question. The Item A exception does not depend on the spouse's residence.

findings.who: A New York City resident whose estranged spouse refuses to sign a joint New York return. The couple have lived apart for twelve months, and during 2025 the spouse lived in New Jersey, or moved out of the city partway through the year.
findings.why_no: The objective evidence of alienation the instructions require, such as 'living apart for the twelve months', usually means the spouse did not live in New York City for all of 2025. The filer truthfully answers no, so the refusal question is never reached.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 5, Item A: "your spouse refuses to sign a joint New York return; ... objective evidence of alienation from your spouse such as: ... living apart for the twelve months immediately preceding application to file a separate return"
findings.fix: Ask the refusal and whereabouts question first, for all married filers who filed a joint federal return. A yes records the line as 'Unable to file jointly' whatever the spouse's residence.

findings.who: A Manhattan resident whose spouse lived all of 2025 in Nassau or Westchester County. Both are full-year New York State residents, so the one-spouse-nonresident exception does not apply. The spouse refuses to sign a joint return.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about New York City, but the Item A exceptions turn on New York State residence and on inability to file jointly. The spouse did not live in the City, so the filer truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 4, Item A: "One spouse is a New York State resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident"; p. 5: "your spouse refuses to sign a joint New York return ... you may file a separate New York return"
findings.fix: Separate the State question from the City question: (1) Was your spouse a New York State resident for all of 2025? (2) Was your spouse also a New York City resident for all of 2025? Ask the cannot-sign question regardless of the answers to either.

findings.who: A New York City resident whose spouse was domiciled in New York City but was physically away all or most of 2025, for example on military deployment, on a work posting abroad, in a hospital or care facility outside the city, or incarcerated. The spouse cannot be reached, or refuses to sign.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'live in New York City for all of 2025' as physical presence rather than residence or domicile. Neither the question nor its help defines residence, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 5, Item A: "the address or whereabouts of your spouse is unknown ... your spouse refuses to sign a joint New York return ... you may file a separate New York return"
findings.fix: Ask whether the spouse was a New York City resident (domiciled there, even if temporarily away) for all of 2025. Add help that points to the instructions' definition of Resident.

findings.who: A filer whose spouse lived in New York City until dying in 2025, filing jointly as surviving spouse.
findings.why_no: 'For all of 2025' suggests no, because the spouse did not live in the city after death. A decedent's year of residence ends at death, so the joint return remains a full-year resident return.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 4: "If the taxpayer whose name is listed second died after December 31, 2024, and before you filed your return, enter the date of death in the box labeled Spouse's date of death."
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'If your spouse died in 2025, answer about the part of the year before their death.'

findings.who: Any filer reading the help shown with the gate.
findings.why_no: The help says a no leads to 'separate returns or a joint return taxing both as residents' and that the tool does not prepare either. This presents the refusal as about residence only. It hides that a separate return is also allowed when a spouse refuses to sign or cannot be found, a case the gated line is meant to record. The line's own condition also says 'full-year New York State and New York City resident', but the gate asks only about the City.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 5, Item A: "You are unable to file a joint New York return because: ... In this case, you may file a separate New York return"
findings.fix: Use the same wording for the gate and the line condition, either 'New York State and New York City resident' in both or 'New York City' in both. Mention the refusal and whereabouts exception in the help, or ask about it separately.

findings.who: A sole proprietor bought a 6,500-pound SUV and other equipment in 2023 and elected section 179 on both. The business income limit created a carryover, and part of it is deducted on the 2025 Form 4562 line 12.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether the carryover 'came from expensing an SUV'. Form 4562 carries the carryover forward as one undivided amount. Under the section 179 regulations, the taxpayer chooses which properties and portions make up the carryover. A filer who never made or recorded that choice cannot trace the carryover to the SUV, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 11, A-208: "If you claimed an IRC § 179 deduction on your federal return with respect to a sport utility vehicle that weighs more than 6,000 pounds ... then enter the amount of that deduction."
findings.fix: Ask a fact the filer can check: 'Was an SUV over 6,000 pounds among the property you (or your spouse) elected to expense under section 179 in the year this carryover arose?' Treat yes as a Yes, or ask how the carryover was allocated among properties.

findings.who: A contractor expensed a pickup over 6,000 pounds GVWR with a bed under six feet, or a heavy passenger van, in 2024. Part of that section 179 carryover is deducted in 2025.
findings.why_no: The help says to count 'any passenger vehicle over 6,000 pounds that is not a truck, van or motor home'. The filer reads 'truck' or 'van' and answers no. A-208 says only 'sport utility vehicle' and gives no blanket exclusion for trucks or vans. Under the federal section 179(b)(5) definition, a short-bed pickup or a van seating nine or fewer behind the driver is treated as an SUV.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 11, A-208: "with respect to a sport utility vehicle that weighs more than 6,000 pounds"
findings.fix: Drop the blanket truck and van exclusion from the help, or state the statutory definition. For example: 'include pickups with a cargo bed under six feet and vans that seat nine or fewer behind the driver'.

findings.who: A filer expensed an SUV whose curb weight is about 5,000 pounds but whose gross vehicle weight rating is over 6,000 pounds. A carryover from that deduction is used in 2025.
findings.why_no: The question and help say 'over 6,000 pounds'. The filer checks the curb or shipping weight, finds it is under 6,000 pounds, and answers no. The 6,000-pound threshold for SUVs is measured by gross vehicle weight rating.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 11, A-208: "a sport utility vehicle that weighs more than 6,000 pounds"
findings.fix: Say 'gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR, shown on the door-jamb label) over 6,000 pounds'.

findings.who: A business owner expensed an SUV in an earlier year and uses it only for business.
findings.why_no: The help calls it a 'passenger vehicle'. The filer thinks of it as a work vehicle, not a passenger car, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 11, A-208: "If you claimed an IRC § 179 deduction ... with respect to a sport utility vehicle"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'including an SUV used only for business'.

locators: p. 11, A-208, "If you claimed an IRC § 179 deduction on your federal return with respect to a sport utility vehicle that weighs more than 6,000 pounds"
p. 11, A-208, "then enter the amount of that deduction"

findings.who: A filer (or joint filer and spouse) with no New York estimated tax payments on line 75, whose only prepayment is wage withholding that is less than the required annual payment—for example, a wage earner with a large bonus or investment income, or a self-employed filer with no withholding.
findings.why_no: The computed gate requires 'Estimated tax payments (line 75) more than zero'; with line 75 at zero it is false, so the tool never asks whether any estimated installment was skipped and treats the late/short-installment line as no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 81: 'You may owe an estimated tax penalty if you did not have enough tax withheld from your wages or did not make enough estimated tax payments on other income you earned during the year.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: ask the late/short-installment question whenever total 2025 prepayments (withholding plus estimated payments, including payments made on the filer's behalf) may be below the required annual payment, or whenever line 80 is $300 or more and more than 10% of the tax; treat zero estimated payments as skipped installments when an installment was required.

locators: p. 23, Line 81, "if you underpaid your estimated tax liability for any payment period"

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse's employer provided dependent care benefits (for example, through the spouse's dependent care FSA, W-2 box 10), or only the spouse paid the daycare provider from the spouse's own account.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from the f2441 helpers 'Did you pay for the care of a qualifying person so you could work or look for work?' and 'Did you receive dependent care benefits?', which say only 'you'. The filer truthfully answers no for themselves. The displayed text says 'you (or your spouse)', but the inputs that drive the condition do not.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'The care was provided so you (and your spouse, if you were married) could work or look for work.'; 'Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits.'
findings.fix: Word both f2441 helpers as 'Did you or your spouse pay for…' and 'Did you or your spouse receive dependent care benefits (for example, Form W-2 box 10 or a dependent care FSA)?', or ask a per-return gate that names the spouse.

findings.who: An employee whose employer paid the care provider directly, ran an on-site daycare, or reimbursed care through a dependent care FSA funded by salary reduction. The employee never handed over money for care and never thinks of having 'received' a benefit.
findings.why_no: 'Did you pay for the care' reads as no because the FSA or employer paid. 'Did you receive dependent care benefits' reads as no because no cash was received, and nothing points the filer to Form W-2 box 10.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits.'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Include care paid through a dependent care FSA or flexible spending plan, care your employer paid for or provided on site, and any amount in Form W-2 box 10.'

findings.who: A filer who paid for care of a disabled spouse or a disabled adult dependent (for example, a parent living with them) so they could work. Or a filer whose child turned 13 during 2025, with care paid for the months before the birthday.
findings.why_no: 'Care of a qualifying person' and 'child and dependent care' read as childcare for young children. The filer does not see adult care or the part-year care of a child who turned 13 as covered.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'Your spouse who is disabled and not able to care for themself and lived with you for more than half the year.'; 'If the child turned 13 during the year, the child is a qualifying person for the part of the year they were under age 13.'
findings.fix: Add help: 'A qualifying person includes a child under 13 (for the part of the year under 13), a disabled spouse, or a disabled person who lived with you more than half the year and whom you claim or could claim as a dependent.'

findings.who: A working parent who paid for summer day camp, a before- or after-school program, preschool or nursery school, or a grandparent or other relative (not a dependent) who babysat while the parents worked.
findings.why_no: These payments are not perceived as 'care expenses'. Camp and after-school programs read as activities, preschool reads as education, and paying a relative reads as informal family help.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: 'The person who provided the care was not your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child under age 13, or a person whom you can claim as a dependent. If your child (including stepchild or foster child) provided the care, they must have been age 19 or older by December 31.'
findings.fix: Add help listing examples: 'daycare, preschool, before/after-school programs, day camp (not overnight camp), and paid babysitters, including relatives who are not your dependents.'

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 paid a provider's bill for care given in late 2024, or who prepaid in 2024 for care provided in 2025.
findings.why_no: A filer who reads the helper as asking about 2025 care paid in 2025 answers no when the payment and the care fall in different years.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 19, Line 64: 'Would you qualify to claim the federal child and dependent care credit for 2025 (whether or not you actually claimed it)?'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Answer yes if you paid in 2025 for care given in an earlier year, or if care given in 2025 was paid earlier.'

locators: p. 1, Who qualifies, "If you qualify to claim the federal child and dependent care credit, you can claim the New York State credit (whether you actually claim the federal credit or not)." and "The care was provided so you (and your spouse, if you were married) could work or look for work." and "Caution: Taxpayers who receive dependent care benefits from their employer must complete Worksheet 1 – Dependent care benefits."

findings.who: A retired employee of the District of Columbia or of a U.S. territory or possession (for example, Puerto Rico) who receives a government pension included in federal AGI on IT-201 line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The question asks only about 'the federal government, the military, or a New York State or local government job'; a DC or territorial government pension is none of those, and the help does not mention them.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'The United States, its territories, possessions (or political subdivisions thereof), ... or the District of Columbia.'
findings.fix: Ask about a 'federal, military, New York State or local, District of Columbia, or U.S. territory/possession government job' and repeat the list in the help.

findings.who: A retiree whose pension is from the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program, MABSTOA, or the Long Island Rail Road and is included in federal AGI on line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The question says 'New York State or local government job'; a public authority such as the MTA, MABSTOA, or LIRR is not the state or a local government, and the help names no public authority.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'Certain public authorities, including: • Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) Police 20-Year Retirement Program; • Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority (MABSTOA); and • Long Island Railroad Company.'
findings.fix: Name the MTA Police 20-Year Retirement Program, MABSTOA, and LIRR in the question or help, or ask about a 'New York public authority' pension.

findings.who: A retired SUNY/CUNY or State Education Department employee in the Optional Retirement Program whose pension is an annuity paid by TIAA or another insurer and is included in federal AGI on line 9 or 10.
findings.why_no: The question asks about a 'New York State ... government job,' but the filer sees a TIAA/insurer annuity and the help does not mention the Optional Retirement Program or TIAA; they read it as a private annuity, not a government pension.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'New York State, including State and City University of New York and New York State Education Department employees who belong to the Optional Retirement Program.'
findings.fix: Mention the Optional Retirement Program and the TIAA example in the help, or ask about 'an ORP annuity paid by TIAA or another insurer.'

findings.who: A joint filer who personally has no IRA, pension, or annuity income, but whose spouse has taxable government pension income on line 9 or 10 (or a disability pension in federal wages on line 1h).
findings.why_no: The gate helper asks 'Is there taxable IRA, pension or annuity income on line 9 or 10?' without 'you or your spouse'; the filer answers for themselves and says no, so the government pension question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9: 'Did you receive a pension or other distribution ... that was included in your federal adjusted gross income?'
findings.fix: Add 'you or your spouse' to both gate helpers: line 9/10 income and line 1h disability pension.

used.revision: Form IT-201-I (2025), Instructions for Form IT-201 (including instructions for Forms IT-195 and IT-201-ATT), 41 pages; final 2025 edition; PDF modified 2025-11-20
locators: p. 9, Line 26, "Did you receive a pension or other distribution from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan that was included in your federal adjusted gross income?"

findings.who: A retired service member, or the surviving spouse of one, who gets military retired pay or a Survivor Benefit Plan annuity on a Form 1099-R from DFAS. Or a retiree of a federal instrumentality such as the Postal Service or TVA, paid under that agency's own name.
findings.why_no: They answer no to the 'federal government pension plan' question because they think of military retired pay as pay, not a 'plan' (or think of the USPS as not 'the government'). The follow-up's list (MTA, MABSTOA, LIRR, SUNY/CUNY/SED, territories, D.C.) names no military or federal agency, so they read it as complete and answer no again.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'The United States, its territories, possessions (or political subdivisions thereof), or any agency or instrumentality of the United States (including the military), or the District of Columbia.'
findings.fix: Add to the follow-up: 'military retired pay or survivor benefits (DFAS), or a pension from any federal agency or instrumentality such as the Postal Service.'

findings.who: A retired New York public school teacher, police officer, firefighter, or county or town worker. They are paid by NYSTRS, NYCERS, the NYC Police or Fire Pension Fund, or a fire or school district plan, and the 1099-R names the retirement system rather than a government.
findings.why_no: They read 'New York State or local government pension plan' as the State itself and do not see the retirement system as 'government'. The follow-up names only the MTA, LIRR, SUNY/CUNY/SED and territories, so it does not catch them.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: '– Local governments within the state.'
findings.fix: Add to the follow-up: 'a New York public retirement system such as NYSLRS, NYSTRS, NYCERS, TRS, BERS, or a police, fire, school district, county, city, town or village plan.'

findings.who: A former New York State or local, or federal, employee who left before retiring and took a refund of their own contributions. The refund was included in AGI and not rolled over.
findings.why_no: They read 'pension' as retirement income and do not see a refund of their own contributions as one. Both questions ask 'from' a plan, and nothing mentions refunds or return of contributions.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'any distributions made to you from a pension plan that represents a return of contributions in a year prior to retirement'
findings.fix: Add: 'Include a refund of your contributions paid when you left public employment before retiring.'

findings.who: A former spouse who gets part of an ex-spouse's NYSLRS, NYC, MTA or federal (OPM or military) pension under a QDRO or a New York DRO.
findings.why_no: The pension was earned by the ex-spouse, so they treat it as not their own government pension. Neither question mentions payments received as a nonemployee spouse under a court order.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26, Nonemployee spouses: 'You may include distributions you received from a New York State or local pension plan or from a federal government pension plan as a nonemployee spouse in accordance with a court-issued qualified domestic relations order (QDRO)...'
findings.fix: Add: 'Include payments you receive under a divorce or domestic relations order (QDRO/DRO) from a public plan earned by a former spouse.'

findings.who: A retiree of a Puerto Rico municipality, or of another political subdivision or agency of a U.S. territory or possession.
findings.why_no: The question says 'the government of a U.S. territory', which they read as the territorial government only, not a municipality or agency within it.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'its territories, possessions (or political subdivisions thereof)'
findings.fix: Say 'the government of a U.S. territory or possession, or any city, town or agency within one'.

findings.who: Joint filers where only the spouse has a CUNY TIAA (ORP) annuity or an LIRR pension, and the filer answering has a private IRA.
findings.why_no: 'Was any of it from...' leaves unclear whose income 'it' means. The answering filer may think only of their own IRA.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: 'as an officer, employee, or beneficiary of an officer or employee of any of the following'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was any pension or distribution received by you or your spouse from...'

locators: p. 9, Line 26, "Did you receive a pension or other distribution from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan that was included in your federal adjusted gross income?"

findings.who: A farmer who files federal Schedule F, has no Schedule C, and rents out nothing. In 2022 they took bonus depreciation on a tractor still used in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about a Schedule C or about renting out property or receiving royalties. A Schedule F filer truthfully has neither, so the 168(k) question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i pp. 20–21, S-213: "New York State does not follow the federal depreciation rules for IRC § 168(k) property placed in service inside or outside New York State on or after June 1, 2003. If you claimed a depreciation deduction for such property ... then complete Part 1 of Form IT-398"
findings.fix: Widen the gate to any depreciation or amortization on the federal return (Form 4562 filed now or in any year since 2003). That includes Schedule F, Form 4835 and Form 2106, and partnership, S corporation and trust K-1s. At minimum, add 'or a Schedule F' to the helper.

findings.who: A partner or S corporation shareholder with no Schedule C and nothing rented in their own name. Their K-1 includes depreciation on 168(k) property, and the entity supplies a New York 168(k) amount for S-213.
findings.why_no: They do not themselves 'rent out, offer for rent' anything they own or lease, and they have no Schedule C. Pass-through business or rental income on Schedule E, Part II does not match either helper.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 21, S-213: "Partners, shareholders, and beneficiaries: Do not complete Form IT-398 to determine the amount to enter. Enter the amount provided to you by the entity of which you are a partner, shareholder, or beneficiary"
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'Did you (or your spouse) receive a federal Schedule K-1 from a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust?' Then ask whether the K-1 or entity statement reports a New York IRC § 168(k) modification (S-213 or S-214).

findings.who: An estate or trust beneficiary whose share of the fiduciary adjustment includes 168(k) depreciation on trust-owned business or rental property. The beneficiary has no Schedule C and rents nothing.
findings.why_no: A beneficiary neither owns nor rents the trust's property, so they truthfully answer no to both helpers.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 21, S-213: "Partners, shareholders, and beneficiaries: ... Enter the amount provided to you by the entity of which you are a partner, shareholder, or beneficiary"
findings.fix: Include estate and trust K-1s in the gate as above, or route them through the fiduciary adjustment (EA-901/ES-901) with the same refusal.

findings.who: A filer who closed a Schedule C business or stopped renting a property in 2024. In 2025 they sold equipment or the building on which they had taken bonus depreciation, reporting the sale only on Form 4797.
findings.why_no: The rental helper asks 'In 2025, did you ... rent out, offer for rent' and the Schedule C helper looks only at the current return. Both are truthfully no for 2025, but the S-214 disposition adjustment applies, and the gated question's Yes would have ended the New York part.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 21, S-214: "If you disposed of IRC § 168(k) property placed in service inside or outside New York State on or after June 1, 2003 ... and your total federal depreciation deduction was more than the New York depreciation deduction for that property, then complete Part 2 of Form IT-398"
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'In 2025, did you sell, exchange, or otherwise dispose of property you had depreciated for a business, rental or farm (for example, on Form 4797)?'

findings.who: An Armed Forces reservist, qualified performing artist, or fee-basis state or local official. They claim unreimbursed employee expenses on Form 2106, including bonus depreciation on a vehicle in an earlier year, and have no Schedule C or rental.
findings.why_no: Their depreciation is on Form 2106, not a Schedule C or rental, so both helpers are a truthful no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i pp. 20–21, S-213: "If you claimed a depreciation deduction for such property ... then complete Part 1 of Form IT-398"
findings.fix: Make the gate depend on any depreciation claimed (any Form 4562 or Form 2106 vehicle depreciation since June 1, 2003), not on Schedule C or rental.

findings.who: A filer who took bonus depreciation on property placed in service from January to May 2003, or who took it on property fully written off and disposed of before 2025 but still carries an IT-398 schedule.
findings.why_no: 'Since 2003' does not match the June 1, 2003 cutoff, and 'still had in 2025' can be read to exclude property fully deducted earlier. The help partly covers this ('count property deducted in full'), but not the date.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 21, S-213: "IRC § 168(k) property placed in service inside or outside New York State on or after June 1, 2003"
findings.fix: Say 'placed in service on or after June 1, 2003' and add 'or that you sold or disposed of in 2025'.

findings.who: A filer (or the filer's spouse on a joint return) who is only the beneficiary of a New York 529 account owned by someone else, and who in 2025 received a withdrawal from that account that was partly included in federal adjusted gross income.
findings.why_no: The gate counts persons who had a 529, Coverdell, or ABLE account, and the gated question asks whether the filer owns a New York 529 account. The help says an account someone else owns for you counts as No. A beneficiary who does not own the account answers No, so the tool treats the line 30 amount as zero.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10: Beneficiary During 2025, did you, as a beneficiary, receive a withdrawal from one or more tuition savings accounts established under New York’s 529 college savings program? ... enter that amount on line 30.
findings.fix: Broaden the gate and the question to cover both account owners and beneficiaries: ask whether the filer or spouse owned a New York 529 account or received a beneficiary withdrawal in 2025, and compute line 30 from contributions plus any qualified distribution included in federal AGI.

findings.who: A farmer who operates a sole proprietorship on Schedule F and holds Build America Bonds in the farm's brokerage account, with the interest reported as other farm income on Schedule F so it is included in federal AGI on IT-201 line 12, while lines 2, 3, 6 and 11 are zero.
findings.why_no: The gate lists only lines 2, 3, 6 and 11 and calls line 6 'business income'; the farmer's farm business income is on line 12, not in the list, so the computed condition is false and the tool never asks about Build America Bonds.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 5, Item G, Code A6: 'Enter this code if you included Build America Bond interest in your federal adjusted gross income.'
findings.fix: Broaden the BAB gate to include line 12 (farm income) and other federal AGI lines, or ask directly whether Build America Bond interest was included in federal AGI.

findings.who: A married filer filing a joint IT-201 whose spouse received a New York inflation refund check in fall 2025 and included it in the joint federal AGI as a state tax refund or other income; the filer personally did not receive or include it.
findings.why_no: The gate says "A state tax refund or other income on federal Schedule 1" and does not say "you or your spouse." The filer reads "you" as self alone and answers no, so the tool never asks the inflation-check question.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Word the gate "you or your spouse" and compute it from the joint Schedule 1 lines; if either spouse received and included the check, the gate must be true.

findings.who: A self-employed filer who deposited the New York inflation refund check into a business account and reported it as gross business income on Schedule C, so it flows to federal Schedule 1 line 3 and into federal AGI, with no state tax refund on line 1 and no amount on line 9.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only for a state tax refund or other income on Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9. The filer truthfully says no because the check was business income, not a state refund or Schedule 1 "other income."
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to ask whether the filer or spouse received a New York inflation refund check and included it in federal AGI, regardless of the federal line or schedule used; do not restrict it to Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9.

findings.who: A filer who included the New York inflation refund check as other income on federal Schedule 1 but also has an equal negative other-income or loss amount, so Schedule 1 line 9 nets to exactly zero.
findings.why_no: The computed gate requires line 9 to be not zero. The check amount is included in federal AGI, but the net line 9 is zero, so the tool computes the gate false and never asks about the check.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Gate on the presence or gross amount of the inflation check itself, or on any Schedule 1 line containing it, not on whether the net line 9 is nonzero.

findings.who: A filer whose gate is true because of an unrelated state tax refund on Schedule 1 line 1, and who also received the New York inflation refund check but included it in federal AGI as business income on Schedule C/Schedule 1 line 3.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks whether the check was included "as a state tax refund or as other income." The filer reads that list as exhaustive and answers no because it was included as business income, not in either named category.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Remove the "as a state tax refund or as other income" limitation and ask whether the filer included the New York inflation refund check in federal income or federal AGI in any manner.

findings.who: A filer whose preparer reported the New York inflation refund check as additional wages on Form 1040 line 1a or as interest on line 2b, so the check is in federal AGI but there is no Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9 amount.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about federal Schedule 1. The filer truthfully says no to having a Schedule 1 state refund or other income, even though the check is included in federal AGI.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 25: "If you received an inflation refund check from the Tax Department and included the check amount in the calculation of federal adjusted gross income reported on line 19, then enter that amount on line 25."
findings.fix: Ask directly about receipt and inclusion in federal AGI rather than using Schedule 1 line 1 or line 9 as a proxy for inclusion.

findings.who: A New York City or Yonkers resident, or a self-employed filer in the MCTD who owes MCTMT. They want this year's overpayment credited to their 2026 city, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax.
findings.why_no: The question says "your 2026 New York tax" and the help says "New York estimated tax". A filer may read this as New York State income tax only, so they answer no and plan to pay the city, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimate separately.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your New York State, New York City, Yonkers, and metropolitan commuter transportation mobility tax estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Ask: "Do you or your spouse want any of your New York overpayment applied to your 2026 New York State, New York City, Yonkers, or MCTMT estimated tax instead of refunded?"

findings.who: Spouses filing a joint return. One spouse makes the 2026 estimated payments, and the other spouse answers the tool's questions.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether "you" want "your" refund kept. The answering spouse does not plan to pay estimated tax and answers no for the couple.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026."
findings.fix: Say "you or your spouse" on joint returns.

findings.who: A filer with an overpayment on line 77 who plans to direct part of it to NYS 529 accounts on line 78a. They see the rest as a credit, not a "refund".
findings.why_no: The question uses the word "refund", but line 78 is the refund that remains after line 79 is taken out. A filer who expects no check may think they have no "refund" to keep.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 78: "Subtract the amount on line 79 (estimated tax) from line 77. This is the amount available for refund."
findings.fix: Use "overpayment (line 77)" in place of "refund". Show the line 77 amount in the question.

findings.who: A filer with an overpayment on line 77 who is first asked how much of it to apply to 2026 estimated tax and enters the whole overpayment, planning to direct part of it to a 529 account later. Line 78 then computes as zero.
findings.why_no: No answer from the filer is involved; the gate is computed. If the tool asks for the line 79 amount before the 529 question, a full line 79 entry makes line 78 zero, and the 529 question is never shown. The filer never sees that line 78a and line 79 compete for the same line 77 overpayment.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to your ... estimated tax for 2026. The total of lines 78a through 79 should equal the amount on line 77."; Line 78: "Subtract the amount on line 79 (estimated tax) from line 77."

findings.who: A partner in a partnership, or a shareholder in an S corporation, whose entity holds bonds of states other than New York. The entity reports the tax-exempt interest on the K-1 (partnership box 18 code A, S corporation box 16 code A) and gives the New York modification EA-113. The filer had no 1099-INT or 1099-DIV showing tax-exempt interest and left federal line 2a blank.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'Was tax-exempt interest received in 2025?' as asking about their own bonds or brokerage forms. They received nothing in cash and no 1099, so they answer No, and line 2a is zero. The gated question ('Did any of your ... tax-free interest or dividends come from bonds issued outside New York, or from a fund that holds them?') is then never asked. Even if it were asked, it names only bonds and funds, not partnerships or S corporations.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7: 'If you have either of the addition or subtraction modifications in the chart below, relating to your partnership or S corporation income, include the amount on the corresponding line of Form IT-201. ... EA-113 Interest income on state and local bonds and obligations 20'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate with an independent condition: 'Did you (or your spouse) receive a K-1 from a partnership or S corporation that reports tax-exempt interest or New York modification EA-113?' If yes, ask for the EA-113 amount whatever the federal answer. Also add to the gated question: 'including interest passed through to you on a partnership or S corporation K-1'.

findings.who: A filer with a national tax-free bond fund who reads the help text before answering the gated question.
findings.why_no: The help text says 'A Yes ends the New York part here.' A filer may read this as saying a Yes takes them out of the New York addition, or that Yes is the wrong answer for New York purposes. They answer No to stay in the New York interview, which drops the interest.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7, Line 20: 'If Yes, enter any such interest income that you received or that was credited to you during 2025 that was not included in your federal adjusted gross income.'
findings.fix: Replace with: 'If Yes, you will be asked for the amount, which New York adds to your income.'

findings.who: A filer holding a bond issued by another state's authority, bought through a New York broker or from a New York-based fund family.
findings.why_no: 'Bonds issued outside New York' can be read as where the bond was sold or held, not as who issued it. The help text lists only New York, its cities and agencies, and U.S. territories as No, so the filer may treat a bond bought through New York the same way.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7: 'interest income from state and local bonds and obligations from states other than New York State or its local governments'
findings.fix: Reword to: 'issued by a state other than New York, or by a city, county, or agency of another state (wherever you bought it)'.

locators: p. 7, Line 20, "Do you have interest income from state and local bonds and obligations from states other than New York State or its local governments?"
p. 7, Line 20, "If Yes, enter any such interest income that you received or that was credited to you during 2025 that was not included in your federal adjusted gross income."

findings.who: A former railroad worker, or the spouse on a joint return, who drew only sickness benefits from the Railroad Retirement Board under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act in 2025 and no unemployment benefits. The Board reports taxable sickness benefits on Form W-2, so they go into federal wages (IT-201 line 1), and line 14 is $0.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as line 14 > $0. Railroad sickness benefits are federal wages, not unemployment compensation, so line 14 is $0 and the question is never asked. The tool treats the line as no and finishes the return without stopping.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i (2025) p. 17, S-122: "benefits received under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act that are exempt from state income taxes under federal laws (but that you included in your federal income)"
findings.fix: Ask the railroad question on its own, not only when line 14 > $0: "Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) receive any unemployment or sickness benefits from the Railroad Retirement Board (Form 1099-G or Form W-2 issued by the RRB)?" Or open the gate when line 14 > $0 OR line 1 > $0.

findings.who: A joint filer whose line 14 holds state unemployment for one spouse, while the other spouse received RUIA sickness benefits from the Railroad Retirement Board, reported as wages on an RRB Form W-2.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether "unemployment benefits" were "paid by the Railroad Retirement Board". The household's unemployment benefits came from the state, and the RRB money was sickness benefits, so the truthful answer is no. The help text mentions sickness benefits only as a statement, not as part of the question.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i (2025) p. 17, S-122: "Certain railroad retirement income and railroad unemployment insurance benefits ... benefits received under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act"
findings.fix: Word the question as: "Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) receive any unemployment or sickness benefits paid by the Railroad Retirement Board under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act, whether reported on Form 1099-G or Form W-2?"

findings.who: A filer whose railroad unemployment benefits were reported on a Form 1099-G from the Railroad Retirement Board but who thinks of the payer as their railroad employer, a union, or 'the railroad unemployment program', not 'the Railroad Retirement Board'.
findings.why_no: "paid by the Railroad Retirement Board" names one issuer. A filer who does not recognize the RRB as the payer, or who counts the benefits as ordinary state unemployment, may answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i (2025) p. 17, S-122: "benefits received under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act ... (but that you included in your federal income)"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Railroad unemployment and sickness benefits are paid by the U.S. Railroad Retirement Board (RRB), not by New York State. Check whether your Form 1099-G or Form W-2 shows the RRB as the payer."

locators: p. 17, S-122, "benefits received under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act that are exempt from state income taxes under federal laws (but that you included in your federal income)"

findings.who: A low-income tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation pays monthly maintenance of more than $450, which includes the co-op's real property taxes, and the unit's market value is $85,000 or less.
findings.why_no: They do not pay rent and do not own real estate in the ordinary sense; they own shares and pay maintenance, so both branches of the question read false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, Step 4: 'A condominium, a cooperative, or a rental unit within a single dwelling is also a residence'; p. 2, line 15: 'Real property taxes paid also include any real estate taxes allowed ... as a deduction for tenant-stockholders in a cooperative housing corporation under IRC section 216.'
findings.fix: Ask about rent, co-op maintenance/tenant-stockholder status, or owning a home, condo, mobile home, or other real estate; state that the $450 rent cap does not apply to homeowners/co-op owners.

findings.who: A low-income filer owns a mobile home that is assessed for real property tax and pays the taxes, but rents the lot for more than $450 a month; the mobile home's market value is $85,000 or less.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether they pay rent of $450 or less or own real estate of $85,000 or less; they do not own land/real estate in the ordinary sense and their lot rent is over $450.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, Step 4: 'A trailer or mobile home that is used only for residential purposes is also a residence if the trailer or mobile home is assessed for real property tax purposes'; 'Mobile homeowners who pay the real property taxes should follow the instructions for homeowners.'
findings.fix: Ask about owning a house, condominium, cooperative shares, or an assessed mobile home/trailer, and about real property taxes paid, not just rent or real estate.

findings.who: A low-income renter pays $500 a month including heat; after subtracting the heat charge, adjusted rent is $440, and the filer is not a dependent.
findings.why_no: They compare the $500 paid to the $450 limit and answer no, because they do not have a separate heat charge or do not treat the parenthetical as a computation.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, line 12: 'Adjusted rent is the rent paid after subtracting any charges for heat, gas, electricity, furnishings, and board.'
findings.fix: Ask for adjusted rent after subtracting those charges, with a 'don't know' path and an example.

findings.who: A low-income renter occupied one New York apartment for seven months at $400 a month and another for five months at $800 a month; the first residence meets the six-month and rent tests, but the annual average rent exceeds $450.
findings.why_no: They average all 2025 rent and answer no, even though the instructions apply the rent limit per rented property and the six-month test to the first residence.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: 'The average monthly rent you or your spouse ... paid was $450 or less'; p. 1 note: 'If the current average monthly rent paid for a rented property ... was more than $450, then no credit is allowed for any renters of that rented property'; p. 2, line 12: 'If you moved from one rented residence to another rented residence, calculate the adjusted rent for each residence.'
findings.fix: Ask on a per-residence basis whether any New York residence occupied six months or more had adjusted rent of $450 or less; do not use a blended annual average.

findings.who: A low-income renter shares an apartment; the total rent is $900 a month, but the filer's share is $450 or less and the filer paid only that share.
findings.why_no: They read 'pay rent averaging $450 a month or less' as the apartment's total rent, not the rent the filer actually paid after the roommate's share.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2, line 11: 'Enter the total rent you or your spouse ... paid during 2025'; line 12: 'Adjusted rent is the rent paid after subtracting any charges...'
findings.fix: Ask for the rent paid by the filer/spouse, after reimbursements from roommates, not the household's total rent.

findings.who: A low-income homeowner's house has a current market value of $80,000 and a mortgage of $70,000; the filer thinks the bank owns the home or that 'worth' means net equity.
findings.why_no: They read 'own real estate worth $85,000 or less' as requiring outright ownership or using equity rather than current market value.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: 'The current market value of all real property you owned ... was $85,000 or less'; p. 1 note: 'If the current market value of a real property is more than $85,000...'
findings.fix: Ask about current market value, not equity or mortgage balance, and state that a mortgage does not mean the filer does not own the home.

locators: p. 1, Do I qualify for this credit?, "Your federal adjusted gross income was $18,000 or less."

findings.who: A general partner or member of an LLC taxed as a partnership, such as a Manhattan law-firm partner, with $200,000 of net earnings from self-employment reported on Schedule K-1 and no Schedule C. On a joint return, the spouse may be the partner.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from Schedule C alone: more than one Schedule C, or Schedule C net profit over $50,000. With no Schedule C the count is zero, the gate is false, and the MCTMT question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "For purposes of the MCTMT, self-employed individuals include: • Sole proprietors • Partners in partnerships • Members of limited liability companies (LLCs) that are treated as partnerships • Partners of limited liability partnerships (LLPs)"
findings.fix: Count a person in the helper if they have any partnership or LLC self-employment earnings (federal Schedule K-1, box 14, code A), or Schedule SE net earnings over $50,000. Simpler: ask whether you or your spouse had any self-employment or partnership earnings from business in the MCTD.

findings.who: A sole proprietor with one Schedule C showing $40,000 net profit in Queens who is also a partner with $30,000 of K-1 self-employment earnings from a Brooklyn partnership. The Zone 1 base from both sources is $70,000.
findings.why_no: The person has exactly one Schedule C and it is under $50,000. The partnership source is not counted, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "You must calculate your MCTMT net earnings base separately for each source of self-employment income ... If you have more than one source, combine all the individual amounts on line 54a (Zone 1 amounts) or line 54b (Zone 2 amounts)"
findings.fix: Make the helper test the combined self-employment earnings for each person across all sources (Schedule C, Schedule F, and partnership K-1), not the count or size of Schedule C forms.

findings.who: A Suffolk or Orange County farmer whose Schedule F shows $90,000 of net farm profit and who has no Schedule C.
findings.why_no: The helper looks only at Schedule C. Farm income goes on Schedule F but is still net earnings from self-employment, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "If an individual’s net earnings from self-employment allocated to either zone exceed $50,000 for the tax year, then you are subject to the MCTMT."
findings.fix: Base the helper on each person's Schedule SE net earnings from self-employment, which covers Schedule C, Schedule F and partnership earnings. Do not base it on Schedule C.

findings.who: A Connecticut-resident partner in a Manhattan partnership, or a consultant whose own office is in New Jersey but whose business is allocated partly to NYC.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether earnings "come from business done in New York City or the nearby counties." The filer thinks of their own work as done elsewhere and does not see that the partnership's or business's allocation percentage puts the earnings in a zone.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "To calculate your MCTMT net earnings base you must multiply your net earnings from self-employment from each source by the specific zone’s allocation percentage for each source"
findings.fix: Ask whether any business or partnership you or your spouse earned self-employment income from had business activity in the five NYC boroughs or the listed counties, wherever you live or work. Then compute or ask the allocated amount.

findings.who: A full-year New York State resident who moved into New York City on July 1, 2025, or moved out of New York City on December 31, 2025, and who has a bonus or installment-sale gain fixed in one year but reported federally in another.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about moving into New York City on January 1, 2025 or out on January 1, 2026. A mid-year or year-end move is a truthful no to both helpers.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'Full-year and part-year New York City residents ... subject ... if you have accrued income for 2025 ... and you were a ... New York City part-year resident for tax year 2025.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to include any New York City part-year resident for 2025, or any change of New York City residency during 2025, not only January 1 moves.

findings.who: A full-year New York State resident who lived outside New York City and moved from New Jersey to Buffalo on January 1, 2025, or from Buffalo to Florida on January 1, 2026, with income fixed in one year but reported federally in another.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about moving into or out of New York City. This filer moved into or out of New York State but not New York City, so both helpers are false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'Full-year New York State residents ... subject ... only if you have accrued income for 2025 and you were a nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024; or you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026.'
findings.fix: Gate on the New York State full-year resident conditions as well as the New York City conditions: nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024 or will be nonresident on January 1, 2026.

findings.who: On a joint return, the filer lived outside New York City all year, but the spouse moved into New York City on January 1, 2025 and has a bonus fixed in one year but reported federally in another.
findings.why_no: The gate helper says 'Moved into New York City' in the singular and does not say 'you or your spouse.' The filer truthfully answers no for himself, even though the spouse's facts trigger the special accrual rules.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'As a full-year New York State resident for 2025, or if you are a full-year New York City resident or New York City part-year resident for 2025, you may have to use special accrual rules ...'
findings.fix: Make the gate per-person on a joint return: ask whether either spouse moved into New York City on January 1, 2025 or out on January 1, 2026, and ask the special-accrual question if either spouse meets the condition.

findings.who: A filer who had a permanent place of abode in New York City throughout 2024 and 2025, was a New York City nonresident on December 31, 2024, but met the 183-day statutory residency test for 2025 and is therefore a full-year New York City resident for 2025, with accrued income fixed in 2024 but reported federally in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the filer 'moved into' New York City on January 1, 2025. This filer did not move; residency changed by statutory days, so the filer answers no even though the legal condition is met.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, Special accruals: 'You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 ... and you were a nonresident of New York City on December 31, 2024, but you were a full-year New York City resident for tax year 2025 ...'
findings.fix: Ask the legal condition directly: were you a New York City nonresident on December 31, 2024 and a full-year New York City resident for 2025, or will you be a New York City nonresident on January 1, 2026, rather than asking only about a move.
