findings.who: A New York resident who contributed $5,000 to their own New York 529 account in 2025 and took nothing out. Federal law gives no deduction for 529 contributions, so nothing about the account appears on the federal return.
findings.why_no: The parent helper asks about 'A 529 plan, Coverdell or ABLE account on the return'. With no Form 1099-Q and nothing federal to report, the filer truthfully answers no. The tool then sets the New York 529 gate to 'No' without ever asking about ownership.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "as an account owner, made contributions, enter the amount up to $5,000 ($10,000 for married taxpayers filing a joint return) on line 1 of the Line 30 worksheet"
findings.fix: Ask about New York 529 ownership, contributions and withdrawals directly for every New York resident filer. Do not route it through a federal 529/Coverdell/ABLE question, because contributions leave no federal trace.

findings.who: A parent who owns a New York 529 account and in 2025 paid $8,000 of private high school tuition from it, paid directly to the school. Federally this is a qualified K-12 distribution. Any Form 1099-Q goes to the student, and nothing is taxable federally.
findings.why_no: Nothing about a 529 appears on the parent's federal return, so the parent answers no to the parent helper about a 529 account 'on the return'. The ownership and nonqualified-withdrawal questions are never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "Nonqualified withdrawals ... include ... any withdrawal used to pay tuition and related expenses in connection with enrollment or attendance at elementary or secondary public, private, or religious schools"
findings.fix: Make the New York 529 gate independent of the federal return. Ask: 'At any time in 2025, did you or your spouse own a New York 529 college savings account, or receive money from one as a beneficiary?'

findings.who: A New York resident college student who is the beneficiary of a grandparent's New York 529 account. In 2025 the student received a distribution whose earnings were partly included in the student's federal AGI.
findings.why_no: The gate helper asks whether the filer 'Owned an account in New York's 529 college savings program'. The beneficiary does not own the account and truthfully answers no. The line 30 question that covers beneficiaries is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "Beneficiary During 2025, did you, as a beneficiary, receive a withdrawal ... If Yes, and you included part of the withdrawal in your federal adjusted gross income ... then enter that amount on line 30."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to 'owned a New York 529 account, or received a withdrawal from one as its beneficiary, in 2025'. Make the gated question ask the beneficiary case explicitly: 'or did you receive money from one as the student/beneficiary?'

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse owns the New York 529 account and made contributions or a withdrawal in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate helper reads 'Owned an account in New York's 529 college savings program' with no 'you or your spouse'. The filer answering the interview thinks of their own accounts and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30 worksheet line 1: "cannot exceed ... $10,000 for married taxpayers filing a joint return"; ny_it225i p. 8, A-103: "include the applicable amounts from all existing accounts owned by you and your spouse"
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'Did you, or (on a joint return) your spouse, own a New York 529 college savings account at any time in 2025?'

findings.who: A New York 529 owner who withdrew money for the student's college, but used it for costs that are not qualified higher education expenses (travel, health insurance), or paid a school that is not an eligible institution. Another example is a withdrawal matching a tax-free scholarship.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether money was taken out 'for anything but college'. The filer sees the withdrawal as 'for college' and answers no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "A withdrawal ... is considered nonqualified unless it is used: • to pay the qualified higher education expenses of the designated beneficiary at an eligible educational institution as defined in Education Law § 695-b(5)"
findings.fix: Replace 'for anything but college' with 'for anything other than qualified higher education expenses (tuition, fees, books, supplies, and eligible room and board) at an eligible college'. Add help that travel, insurance and scholarship-matching withdrawals count as Yes.

findings.who: A filer or couple owning several New York 529 accounts, for example one per child, where the contribution or withdrawal was in an account other than the one they think of first.
findings.why_no: Both questions refer to 'that New York 529 account' in the singular. The filer answers about one account only.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "make contributions to or a withdrawal from one or more tuition savings accounts established under New York's 529 college savings program"
findings.fix: Say 'any New York 529 account you or your spouse own' in both gated questions.

findings.who: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, born between January 1 and July 1, 1966, who received a taxable IRA, 401(k) or private pension distribution in the second half of 2025, after turning 59½ during the year.
findings.why_no: The gate counts only recipients born in 1965 or earlier. Its helper text claims that this means '59½ or older at some time in 2025', but a person born in the first half of 1966 reaches 59½ between July and December 2025. The computed count is therefore 0, and that person is never asked.
findings.line: ny_it201.pension_exclusion_if_young (and the line 29 exclusion or refusal it leads to)
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'If you became 59½ during 2025, enter only the amount you received after you became 59½, but not more than $20,000.'
findings.fix: Count recipients born before July 2, 1966, not 'in 1965 or earlier'. Better, ask the line 29 question whenever any taxable pension, annuity or IRA income exists, and let the filer give the date they turned 59½.

findings.who: A filer under 59½ (born after mid-1966) who received taxable distributions as the beneficiary of a deceased parent's IRA or pension, where the decedent would have qualified for the exclusion.
findings.why_no: The gate checks only the recipient's own birth year, so no recipient is counted. The beneficiary clause exists only inside the gated question, and that question is reached only through this gate. In addition, the line's 'Otherwise: false, and the question below is not asked' means that when the gate is false the question is never asked at all. The beneficiary branch is unreachable.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'If you received pension and annuity income and are married, or received pension and annuity income as a beneficiary, see Married taxpayers or Beneficiaries below.'
findings.fix: Make the gate 'any person had taxable pension, annuity or IRA income' (count > 0), with no age filter. Then ask whether the recipient turned 59½ by December 31, 2025, or received the money as the beneficiary of someone who died.

findings.who: Any filer whose gate evaluates false, that is, every young or beneficiary recipient of private pension or IRA income.
findings.why_no: The line's logic is self-defeating. When the gate holds, the choice resolves to 'No' because a recipient was born in 1965 or earlier. When the gate fails, the line is forced to false and the question is not asked. No path ever asks the question or yields yes.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'Did you enter an amount of pension income or annuity income, or both ... that was not from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan?'
findings.fix: Invert the gate so the question is asked when no recipient is known to be 59½. Alternatively, drop the gate and ask whenever taxable pension, annuity or IRA income exists, since the tool must refuse or compute in either case.

findings.who: A filer 59½ or older whose only qualifying income is periodic distributions from a government 457 plan, a 403(b) or a 401(k), which they do not think of as 'pension or IRA money'.
findings.why_no: The question says 'that pension or IRA money', and the help mentions only 'such income'. A filer with a 401(k) or 457 plan may read this as excluding their plan.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: qualifying income includes 'periodic distributions from government (IRC § 457) deferred compensation plans' and 'a qualified cash or deferred profit-sharing or stock bonus plan [IRC § 401(k)]'.
findings.fix: Name the plan types in the question: 'pension, annuity, IRA, 401(k), 403(b), Keogh, or government 457 plan distributions'.

findings.who: A New York City resident who works for NYC Health + Hospitals, the NYC Transit Authority, MABSTOA, Staten Island Rapid Transit, the NYC School Construction Authority or the Housing Authority. Their W-2 box 14 shows an IRC 125 flexible benefits deduction, and they may also show a 414(h) contribution to NYCERS or the MABSTOA plan.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'a New York public employer.' They think of their employer as a hospital, a transit company or an authority, not as a government. A public benefit corporation does not read as a 'public employer,' so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 7, A-101: 'Certain other New York City public employers may include, but are not limited to, the following: ... NYC Health and Hospitals Corporation • NYC Transit Authority • NYC Housing Authority ... • Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority • Staten Island Rapid Transit Authority'; ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'a member of the Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority (MABSTOA) Pension Plan'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you (or your spouse) get a Form W-2 from New York State, a New York city, county, town, village, school district or BOCES, a state or city university (SUNY or CUNY), or a New York public authority or public benefit corporation (for example the MTA, NYC Transit, MABSTOA, NYC Health + Hospitals or the Housing Authority)?' Add help text saying the list is not complete. Alternatively, ask a broader question: does any W-2 box 14 show 414(h), IRC 125, or a retirement system name such as NYSLRS, TRS, NYCERS, TRS NYC, BERS, ORP or MABSTOA?

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly. Only the spouse works for a New York public employer, for example as a teacher who belongs to the State Teachers' Retirement System, and that W-2 shows a 414(h) contribution or an IRC 125 flex amount.
findings.why_no: The gate cites 'Are you a public employee of New York State or its local governments?' and does not mention a spouse. The filer answering for the return reads 'you' as themselves and says no. Only the gated child questions say 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse).'
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'enter the amount of 414(h) retirement contributions, if shown on any federal Form W-2'; ny_it225i p. 7, A-101: 'If any federal Form W-2 ... shows that an amount was deducted or deferred ... on your or a decedent's behalf'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'Did you or your spouse get a Form W-2 from a New York public employer?' Or compute it over every W-2 on the return, whichever spouse it belongs to, rather than asking one person.

findings.who: A SUNY or CUNY faculty or staff member in the Optional Retirement Program, with TIAA as the carrier, whose W-2 shows a 414(h) ORP contribution. Also a teacher at a charter school that participates in the State Teachers' Retirement System.
findings.why_no: They see themselves as university employees or charter-school employees whose pension is run by TIAA, a private company, not as 'public employees of New York State or its local governments.' They answer no to the public-employer gate even though the line names their retirement plan.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: 'an employee of the State or City University of New York who belongs to the Optional Retirement Program; – a member of the New York State Teachers' Retirement System'
findings.fix: Ask the gate by retirement plan as well as by employer: 'Are you or your spouse a member of NYSLRS, the State Teachers' Retirement System, the SUNY or CUNY Optional Retirement Program (including through TIAA), NYCERS, TRS NYC, BERS, the NYC Police or Fire pension fund, or the MABSTOA plan, or does any W-2 box 14 show 414(h)?'

findings.who: The executor filing a decedent's final IT-201. A New York City public employer issued a W-2 in the decedent's name that shows an IRC 125 flex deduction.
findings.why_no: The flex question asks only about a W-2 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) got.' A fiduciary filing for the decedent may not read 'you' as covering the decedent.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 7, A-101: 'an amount was deducted or deferred from your salary under a flexible benefits program ... on your or a decedent's behalf'
findings.fix: Add 'or the deceased person this return is for' to both the gate and the flex question.
